questions.q: Which property most distinguishes a set from a list?
questions.explain: A set has no duplicates and answers "is x in you?". Mathematically, order does not matter: {Ada, Bola} and {Bola, Ada} are the same set.
options: A set can only hold numbers
A set holds each element at most once, and its main question is membership
A set can hold at most 100 elements

questions.q: A payment service must never process the same order id twice. It receives thousands of ids per minute. What should it keep the processed ids in?
questions.explain: The question asked again and again is membership. has on a set jumps almost straight to the answer; includes on an array checks items one by one, which gets slow as the list grows.
options: A string, with ids separated by commas
A number that counts processed orders

questions.q: How do you get the number of elements in a set called tags?
questions.explain: size is a property, so it has no parentheses. Arrays use length; sets use size.

questions.q: Which expression turns the array ids into an array without duplicates?
questions.explain: new Set(ids) drops the duplicates but gives a set, not an array. Spreading it into [ … ] gives an array back. new Set([ids]) makes a set with one element: the whole array.

questions.q: For any element x, "x is in A ∪ B" is the same as…
questions.explain: Union is OR on membership. Intersection is AND, difference is AND NOT, symmetric difference is XOR.
options: x is in A and x is in B
x is in A or x is in B
x is in A and not in B
x is in exactly one of A and B

questions.q: You want the customers who bought both rice and oil. You have a set of rice buyers and a set of oil buyers. Which operation?
questions.explain: "Both" is AND, and AND on membership is intersection: rice.intersection(oil).

questions.q: Which is true about a.difference(b) and b.difference(a)?
questions.explain: Difference depends on the order, like a && !b versus b && !a. Union and intersection do not depend on the order.
options: They are usually different: the first is "in a, not in b", the second is "in b, not in a"

questions.q: Which customers are in the symmetric difference of the web list and the store list?
questions.explain: Symmetric difference is XOR on membership: in one or the other, but not both.
options: Those on exactly one of the lists

questions.q: Why is there no complement() method on a JavaScript set?
questions.explain: "Customers not on the web list" only makes sense relative to all customers. Supply that universe explicitly and take the difference.
options: Because complements are not part of set theory
Because "everything not in the set" depends on a universe the set cannot know; you write universe.difference(set)
Because sets cannot contain the word "not"

questions.q: required.isSubsetOf(held) is true. What does that mean?
questions.explain: A ⊆ B means every element of A is also in B. B may contain more. "At least one" would be "the intersection is not empty".
options: The user holds exactly the required permissions and no others
Every required permission is among the held permissions
At least one required permission is held

questions.q: A check fails. Which expression tells the user exactly which permissions they are missing?
questions.explain: Missing permissions are those required but not held: in required, not in held. The other order gives the extra permissions the user has.

questions.q: An admin page's required-permission set is accidentally empty. What happens with required.isSubsetOf(held)?
questions.explain: The empty set is a subset of every set: no element can fail the test. An empty requirement means "open to all", so a safe checker refuses empty requirements as a configuration mistake.
options: It is false for everyone, so nobody gets in
It is true for everyone, even users with no permissions
It depends on the order of the elements

questions.q: What does held.isDisjointFrom(banned) check?
questions.explain: Disjoint sets share nothing: their intersection is empty.
options: That held and banned have no element in common
That the sets have different sizes

questions.q: A user has the roles support and warehouse. Which operation combines the two roles' permission sets into the set the user holds?
questions.explain: A user holds a permission if any of their roles grants it: that is OR, so union. Intersection would give only permissions that both roles grant.

questions.q: A user's roles contain a typo, "suport". What should a well-designed permission checker do?
questions.explain: Fail closed: an unknown role adds no permissions. A warning makes the mistake visible instead of silently removing someone's access.
options: Grant every permission, so the user is not blocked
Grant nothing for that role and log a warning so someone can fix it

questions.q: Why does a set containing two separately created { id: 101 } objects have size 2?
questions.explain: Sets decide sameness almost exactly like ===, and === on objects asks "is it the very same object?". Store ids instead to de-duplicate records.
options: Because sets allow duplicates for objects
Because sets compare objects by identity: two separate objects are different, even with the same contents
Because the objects are sorted differently

questions.q: A newsletter set contains "Ada@Mail.com" and "ada@mail.com". What is the fix?
questions.explain: To ===, a capital letter makes a different string. Decide what "the same customer" means, and apply it before the data reaches the set.
options: Normalise emails (trim spaces, lower-case) before adding them to the set
Use an array instead of a set

questions.q: What happens to a set when you pass it straight to JSON.stringify?
questions.explain: JSON has no set type, and a Set has no own properties to save. Convert with [...set] before saving or sending, and rebuild the set when reading.
options: It becomes {}: the elements are lost

questions.q: How can you check that two sets a and b contain exactly the same elements?
questions.explain: Two different set objects are never ===. Equal sizes are not enough: {1, 2} and {3, 4} have the same size. Each being a subset of the other means same elements.

questions.q: A has 30 customers, B has 20, and 5 are in both. How many are in A ∪ B?
questions.explain: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| = 30 + 20 − 5. Adding the sizes counts the 5 shared customers twice.

questions.q: With a universe of all customers, which expression gives the customers on neither the web list nor the store list?
questions.explain: "Neither" is NOT (A OR B), by De Morgan. On sets: the complement of the union, which is the universe minus the union.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: new Set loops over a string's characters: m, a, n, a, g, e, r. The second a is a duplicate, so 6 letters remain, and the word itself is not an element. Pass ["manager"].
questions.code:
const roles = new Set("manager");
console.log(roles.size, roles.has("manager"));

questions.explain: The two objects are different objects, so both stay. The number 7 is added once. That is 3 elements.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The raw strings all differ, so the raw set has 3. After trimming and lower-casing, the two Ada entries become the same string.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A set turns into {} in JSON and its elements are lost. Spread it into an array first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two set objects are never ===, even with the same elements. The mutual subset check compares their contents, and order does not matter.

questions.q: A cart contains repeated product ids. Print the number of distinct products, then the distinct ids as an array.
questions.explain: A set drops the repeats; size counts what is left and spreading turns it back into an array, in first-seen order.
questions.starter:
const cartIds = [12, 7, 12, 3, 7, 12];

// print the number of distinct ids, then the array of distinct ids

questions.q: Write intersect(a, b) by hand, with a loop and has (without the built-in intersection method). It returns a new set of elements in both.
questions.explain: Intersection is AND on membership: keep each element of a that b also has.

questions.q: Print the number of emails to send: everyone on the web or store list, minus the unsubscribed.
questions.explain: (W ∪ S) \ U: the union has ada, bola, chidi, dayo and efe; removing chidi and efe leaves 3.

questions.q: Write checkAccess(held, required): return "refused: nothing required" for an empty requirement, "refused: missing X, Y" listing the missing permissions, or "allowed".
questions.explain: The empty-set guard comes first, because the empty set would otherwise pass as a subset of anything. The difference both decides and explains the refusal.
questions.expected:
allowed
refused: missing orders:delete, reports:read
refused: nothing required

questions.q: Write permissionsOf(roles) that returns the union of the permission sets of the given role names, skipping unknown names. Print the size of the result for ["support", "warehouse", "suport"].
questions.explain: Support and warehouse both grant orders:read, which the union counts once: 2 + 3 − 1 = 4. The misspelled role grants nothing.

questions.q: Write similarity(a, b): the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union, or 0 when both sets are empty.
questions.explain: 2 shared tags out of 4 distinct ones gives 0.5. The guard avoids 0 / 0, which is NaN.

questions.q: Write sameElements(a, b) that returns true when two sets contain exactly the same elements.
questions.explain: Each set contained in the other means the same elements. === would say false even for the first pair, and comparing sizes alone would wrongly accept the second.
